transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Mr. Park, I need to talk with you about your care over the last twenty-four hours. I have some difficult news regarding a mistake that was made.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Oh. Is it about the tests?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Yes. There was an error in how your ECG was handled. The machine flagged an abnormal result right away, but I did not review that result for four hours. Because I didn't see it, we didn't start the necessary treatment for your heart event immediately. Do you follow what I'm saying so far?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I... I don't really know. You mean you just didn't look at it?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is correct. I missed the alert, and that caused a delay in your diagnosis. Does that make sense?

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I guess. I just thought everything was being handled. I've never really been in a hospital by myself before. I'm kind of shaking.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I am sorry. I am the one responsible for this mistake. It was my job to check those results, and I failed to do that in a timely manner.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Is it my fault? Did I do something?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: No, you did absolutely nothing wrong. This was entirely a failure on my part.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: So what does that mean for me now? Like, for my health? Am I going to be okay?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: Because of the delay, there is permanent damage to your heart muscle. This means your heart doesn't pump as efficiently as it should. You will likely have a reduced capacity for exercise and a higher risk of heart failure in the future.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Wait, permanent? I'm nineteen. I can't have heart failure. I have a scholarship for sports. Does this mean I can't play?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand this is a lot to take in, but we need to focus on the medical steps now.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: But you don't understand, my whole life is basically my sport. My parents are going to be so—

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We really need to go over the management plan quickly because I have to go check on another patient in a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't think I can just move on to a plan right now. I'm actually really scared.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: I understand. But looking forward, here is exactly what happens next. First, you are staying in this bed for another forty-eight hours for continuous monitoring. Tomorrow morning at 8:00 AM, the cardiology specialist will visit you to calibrate your new medication dosage. Your role is to track any shortness of breath in this logbook I'm giving you and alert the nurse immediately if you feel a flutter in your chest.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: Will the medicine fix the damage?

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: It won't reverse the damage already done, but it will prevent it from getting worse. Regarding how we stop this from happening again, our department is implementing a new mandatory alert system that pings the attending physician's phone and a backup resident simultaneously if an ECG is flagged. I have already filed a formal incident report to ensure the system is audited.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I don't know what to tell my parents. I don't even know if I should call a lawyer.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: That is certainly your right to do. As for the immediate next steps, the specialist will be here tomorrow, and I will personally bring you a written summary of today's conversation by 5:00 PM today so you have it for your family.

transcript.speaker: Patient
transcript.text: I just can't believe this happened. I feel like I can't breathe.

transcript.speaker: Resident
transcript.text: We have the monitors on you to track that. Let's wrap this up so you can rest before the specialist arrives. Do you have any other questions about the medications?

H.justification: Resident uses rushing language repeatedly ('need to focus on the medical steps now', 'go over the management plan quickly because I have to go', 'Let's wrap this up').

E.justification: Error named in turn 2, used lay language, checked comprehension twice ('Do you follow...', 'Does that make sense?'), and provided no false reassurance.

A.justification: Direct apology used ('I am sorry'), resident explicitly took personal responsibility ('I am the one responsible'), and maintained this under pushback.

R.justification: Resident uses generic validation ('I understand') but does not name specific emotions or engage with the patient's distress regarding their sports scholarship.

T.justification: Provided specific steps with timelines (48 hours, 8:00 AM tomorrow, 5:00 PM today), defined the patient's role (tracking shortness of breath in logbook), and addressed prevention (new alert system).
